courseStage: All new cards are Year 1 mock eligible; earlier A2 cards remain unchanged

cards.front: In a skeletal formula, what does each unlabelled line end represent?
cards.back: One carbon atom.

cards.front: In a skeletal formula, how many bonds does neutral carbon normally make?
cards.back: Four covalent bonds, with omitted C–H bonds implied.

cards.front: Fill the gap: an empirical formula gives the simplest whole-number ___ of atoms.
cards.back: ratio

cards.front: Name CH₃CH(CH₃)CH₂CH₃.
cards.back: 2-methylbutane.

cards.front: Name CH₃CH(OH)CH₂CH₃.
cards.back: Butan-2-ol.

cards.front: When naming an ester, which part of the name comes first?
cards.back: The alkyl part derived from the alcohol.

cards.front: How many carbons are in the parent chain named pent-?
cards.back: Five.

cards.front: Which atom counts as carbon 1 in a carboxylic acid?
cards.back: The carbon atom of the –COOH group.

cards.front: When a C–Br bond breaks heterolytically, where does its curly arrow point?
cards.back: Towards Br, which takes the bonding electron pair.

cards.front: Choose the correct arrow source: A electrophile; B lone pair; C positive charge.
cards.back: B: the lone pair supplying the electrons.

cards.front: How is stereoisomerism different from structural isomerism?
cards.back: Same connectivity but a different arrangement in space.

cards.front: In CIP ranking, if attached atoms tie, what do you compare next?
cards.back: Their attached atoms, ordered by atomic number, until the first difference.

cards.front: CIP: which has higher priority, –CH₂OH or –CH₃?
cards.back: –CH₂OH: its next attached atoms include oxygen.

cards.front: What is a crude-oil fraction?
cards.back: A mixture of hydrocarbons with similar boiling points.

cards.front: Fill the gap: a fractionating column is cooler near the ___.
cards.back: top

cards.front: Where do higher-boiling crude-oil fractions condense?
cards.back: Lower down the hotter fractionating column.

cards.front: Is fractional distillation a chemical change or physical separation?
cards.back: Physical separation; no hydrocarbon molecules are changed.

cards.front: Why do larger alkane molecules generally have higher boiling points?
cards.back: More electrons produce stronger London dispersion forces.

cards.front: Which cracking method uses high temperature and high pressure?
cards.back: Thermal cracking.

cards.front: Fill the gap: catalytic cracking uses a ___ catalyst.
cards.back: zeolite

cards.front: Why can nitrogen oxides form inside combustion engines?
cards.back: High temperatures allow nitrogen and oxygen from air to react.

cards.front: In a catalytic converter, CO is oxidised to which gas?
cards.back: Carbon dioxide, CO₂.

cards.front: In a catalytic converter, nitrogen oxides are reduced to what?
cards.back: Nitrogen, N₂.

cards.front: Complete the flue-gas equation: CaO + SO₂ → ___
cards.back: CaSO₃.

cards.front: Complete the flue-gas equation: CaCO₃ + SO₂ → CaSO₃ + ___
cards.back: CO₂.

cards.front: Radical initiation: fill the gap, Cl₂ → ___ (under UV).
cards.back: 2Cl•

cards.front: Radical propagation 1: Cl• + CH₄ → HCl + ___
cards.back: CH₃•

cards.front: Radical propagation 2: CH₃• + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + ___
cards.back: Cl•

cards.front: What happens next after CH₃• reacts with Cl₂ in propagation?
cards.back: A chlorine radical is regenerated and can continue the chain.

cards.front: Termination: complete CH₃• + CH₃• → ___
cards.back: C₂H₆.

cards.front: Why can methane chlorination give several chlorinated products?
cards.back: The products can undergo further radical substitution.

cards.front: In a radical mechanism, what does a dot after a symbol mean?
cards.back: An unpaired electron, not an ionic charge.

cards.front: A C–X carbon is bonded to two other carbons. Classify the halogenoalkane.
cards.back: Secondary.

cards.front: Substitution arrow 1: OH⁻ attacks which atom of a halogenoalkane?
cards.back: The δ⁺ carbon bonded to the halogen.

cards.front: Substitution arrow 2: where does the C–Br bond's electron pair move?
cards.back: To bromine, which leaves as Br⁻.

cards.front: In nucleophilic substitution by CN⁻, which end forms the C–C bond?
cards.back: The carbon end of CN⁻.

cards.front: Fill the gap: substitution of R–Br with NH₃ first gives R–NH₃___.
What happens after the positively charged RNH₃⁺ intermediate forms?
cards.back: A base removes H⁺, giving a neutral primary amine.

cards.front: In elimination by OH⁻, does OH⁻ attack carbon or an adjacent hydrogen?
cards.back: An adjacent (β) hydrogen; OH⁻ acts as a base.

cards.front: Elimination arrow 1: where does the oxygen lone pair of OH⁻ point?
cards.back: To a hydrogen on the carbon next to the C–Br carbon.

cards.front: Elimination arrow 2: where do the β C–H bonding electrons move?
cards.back: Into the bond between the two carbons, forming C=C.

cards.front: Elimination arrow 3: where do the C–Br bonding electrons move?
cards.back: To Br, forming Br⁻.

cards.front: Elimination of 2-bromobutane: name two possible alkene position isomers.
cards.back: But-1-ene and but-2-ene.

cards.front: Ozone cycle step 1: Cl• + O₃ → ClO• + ___
cards.back: O₂.

cards.front: Ozone cycle step 2: ClO• + O₃ → Cl• + ___
cards.back: 2O₂.

cards.front: What is cancelled when the two chlorine-radical ozone steps are added?
cards.back: Cl• and ClO•, as both are regenerated or intermediates.

cards.front: Complete the net ozone-decomposition equation: 2O₃ → ___
cards.back: 3O₂.

cards.front: An alkene C=C consists of which two bond types?
cards.back: One σ bond and one π bond.

cards.front: Why does a C=C bond restrict rotation?
cards.back: Rotation would disrupt sideways overlap forming the π bond.

cards.front: HBr addition arrow 2: where does the H–Br bond's electron pair go?
cards.back: To bromine, forming Br⁻.

cards.front: After HBr protonates ethene, which charged intermediate forms?
cards.back: The ethyl carbocation, CH₃CH₂⁺.

cards.front: HBr addition final arrow: where does the Br⁻ lone pair point?
cards.back: Towards the positively charged carbon of the carbocation.

cards.front: Why does Br₂ become polarised as it approaches an alkene?
cards.back: The alkene π electrons repel Br₂ electrons, inducing a dipole.

cards.front: What is the product of adding Br₂ to ethene?
cards.back: 1,2-dibromoethane.

cards.front: What is the immediate product of ethene + H₂SO₄?
cards.back: Ethyl hydrogensulfate, CH₃CH₂OSO₃H.

cards.front: After H₂SO₄ protonates ethene, which ion attacks the carbocation?
cards.back: Hydrogensulfate, HSO₄⁻, through oxygen.

cards.front: In the major product from propene + HBr, which carbon bears bromine?
cards.back: Carbon 2 (forming 2-bromopropane).

cards.front: In a polymer repeating-unit diagram, where is n placed?
cards.back: Outside the square brackets.

cards.front: What must pass through both ends of a polymer's repeating-unit brackets?
cards.back: The two continuation bonds.

cards.front: Poly(propene) has which side group on its carbon backbone?
cards.back: A methyl (–CH₃) group.

cards.front: What is the monomer of poly(chloroethene), PVC?
cards.back: Chloroethene, CH₂=CHCl.

cards.front: What is the overall fermentation equation for glucose to ethanol?
cards.back: C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂.

cards.front: What is the reaction type when ethene becomes ethanol with water?
cards.back: Hydration (addition).

cards.front: Which colour change shows Cr₂O₇²⁻ reducing to Cr³⁺ in alcohol oxidation?
cards.back: Orange to green.

cards.front: Which oxidation state does chromium change from/to in dichromate oxidation?
Why use distillation rather than reflux to isolate an aldehyde?
cards.back: Distillation removes the aldehyde before it can oxidise further.

cards.front: Why does reflux prevent loss of volatile reactants?
cards.back: Vapour condenses and returns to the reaction vessel.

cards.front: Alcohol dehydration mechanism step 1: what happens to the –OH group?
cards.back: It is protonated to –OH₂⁺, making water a better leaving group.

cards.front: Alcohol dehydration: after protonation, what group can leave?
cards.back: Water, H₂O.

cards.front: Alcohol dehydration: which proton is removed to form the C=C bond?
cards.back: A β-hydrogen on a carbon next to the former –OH carbon.

cards.front: Alcohol dehydration: what happens to the acid catalyst overall?
cards.back: It is regenerated.

cards.front: Why can dehydration of an unsymmetrical alcohol give different alkenes?
cards.back: A β-hydrogen can be removed from different adjacent carbons.

cards.front: Which test would show an aldehyde but not a typical simple ketone?
cards.back: Tollens' or Fehling's reagent gives a positive result.

cards.front: How can a high-resolution mass spectrum help find a molecular formula?
cards.back: Its precise molecular mass can distinguish elemental compositions.

cards.front: How does an IR spectrum help identify a functional group?
cards.back: Characteristic bonds absorb at characteristic wavenumbers.

cards.front: How can an IR spectrum help reveal an impurity?
cards.back: It may show additional absorption peaks absent from the pure compound.

cards.front: Ammonia substitution: where does the next NH₃ lone-pair arrow point?
cards.back: Towards H on the positively charged RNH₃⁺ intermediate.

cards.front: Ammonia deprotonation: where do the R–NH₃⁺ N–H bond electrons go?
cards.back: Back onto its nitrogen atom, giving the neutral amine.

cards.front: When CN⁻ replaces a halogen in R–X, how does the carbon count change?
cards.back: It increases by one carbon atom.

cards.front: Br₂ addition arrow 1: where do the alkene π electrons move?
cards.back: Towards the induced δ⁺ bromine atom.

cards.front: Br₂ addition arrow 2: where do the Br–Br bonding electrons go?
cards.back: Towards the other Br, forming Br⁻.

cards.front: Ethene + H₂SO₄: what breaks when ethene bonds to H⁺?
cards.back: The acid O–H bond breaks heterolytically to form HSO₄⁻.

cards.front: Complete the monomer: [–CH₂–CH(Cl)–]ₙ comes from ___
cards.back: CH₂=CHCl (chloroethene).

cards.front: During alcohol dehydration, which electrons form the alkene's π bond?
cards.back: A pair from a C–H bond next to the carbon losing water.
